default-145.name: Rambutan and Pineapple Bowl
default-145.instructions: Make a chilled fruit bowl with peeled rambutan, pineapple and lime juice.
default-145.raw: Remove the hairy skin and eat the translucent flesh; discard the seed.

146.name: Longan
146.selectionGuide: Choose intact, firm fruit; the thin shell should not be cracked or mouldy.
146.storageGuide: Refrigerate longan in its shell in a breathable bag; wash and peel just before eating.
146.funFact: Longan is a close relative of lychee and rambutan. Its name means 'dragon eye' in Chinese: pale flesh surrounds a dark seed, resembling an eye. In southern Chinese cuisine it is used fresh and dried, including in infusions.

default-146.name: Chilled Longan Fruit Salad
default-146.instructions: Peel the fruit, remove the seed and add the flesh to a chilled fruit salad.
default-146.raw: Eat only the peeled flesh and discard the seed and skin.

147.name: Feijoa (Pineapple Guava)
147.selectionGuide: Choose fruit with a fragrant scent and slight give; avoid shrivelling.
147.storageGuide: Refrigerate ripe feijoa and use promptly; allow firm fruit to soften at room temperature.
147.funFact: Feijoa originated in South America, and its flowers are edible, with a sweet, slightly spicy flavor. The fruit combines aromas reminiscent of guava, pineapple, and mint, which is why it is also called pineapple guava.

default-147.name: Feijoa Yogurt Bowl
default-147.instructions: Halve ripe fruit and scoop the aromatic flesh into yogurt with honey.
default-147.raw: The fragrant pulp is eaten raw; the skin is also edible but can be tart.

148.name: Sea Buckthorn
148.selectionGuide: Choose plump berries with no leaking juice, mould or crushed fruit at the bottom of the pack. Berries should be plump and orange-yellow; avoid crushed, fermented-smelling fruit.
148.storageGuide: Refrigerate unwashed in a shallow, breathable container. Remove damaged berries and wash gently just before eating.
148.funFact: Sea buckthorn is a pioneer plant that stabilizes soil and thrives in poor, sandy sites. Its orange berries contain oil in both the flesh and seeds, an unusual feature among berry fruits.

default-148.name: Sea Buckthorn Berry Sauce
default-148.instructions: Warm the berries gently with a little water, strain if desired and use the tart purée in a sauce.
default-148.raw: The berries are edible raw but very tart; remove them carefully because the branches are thorny.

149.name: Mulberries
149.selectionGuide: Choose plump berries with no leaking juice, mould or crushed fruit at the bottom of the pack. Choose fully coloured berries that are plump and not leaking.
149.storageGuide: Refrigerate unwashed in a shallow, breathable container. Remove damaged berries and wash gently just before eating.
149.funFact: Mulberries are aggregate fruits, and their leaves have fed silkworms for thousands of years. The mulberry tree's role in sericulture was economically important in China and along the historic Silk Road.

default-149.name: Mulberries with Yogurt
default-149.instructions: Scatter fresh mulberries over yogurt or freeze them in a single layer for later use.
default-149.raw: Rinse gently and eat the ripe berries fresh.

150.name: Elderberries
150.selectionGuide: Choose plump berries with no leaking juice, mould or crushed fruit at the bottom of the pack. Use only correctly identified ripe berries from a food seller; avoid unripe fruit.
150.storageGuide: Refrigerate fresh berries briefly; cook promptly and do not store cooked berries at room temperature.
150.funFact: Elderberries have traditionally been used in European syrups and preserves, but they require proper heat treatment. The plant contains natural cyanogenic compounds, so raw unripe berries and other raw plant parts should not be eaten.

default-150.name: Cooked Elderberry Syrup
default-150.instructions: Remove the berries from the stems and cook into a syrup or sauce; strain out the seeds if desired. Do not eat raw elderberries or other parts of the plant; cook ripe berries thoroughly and discard stems and leaves.

151.name: Jackfruit
151.selectionGuide: Choose a fruit that is sound and fragrant; very large fruit can be sold in cut sections.
151.storageGuide: Keep whole jackfruit in a cool, ventilated place; refrigerate cut fruit covered and use promptly.
151.funFact: Jackfruit is the largest fruit that grows on a tree; an individual fruit can weigh dozens of kilograms. In South Asian cooking, ripe flesh is used in desserts, while unripe fibrous flesh goes into curries and savory dishes.

default-151.name: Ripe Jackfruit Fruit Bowl
default-151.instructions: Separate the ripe bulbs from the fibrous core and serve chilled with lime; remove the seeds.
default-151.raw: Ripe bulbs can be eaten raw; remove the skin, core and seeds. Unripe jackfruit is normally cooked.

152.name: Sweet Chestnuts
152.selectionGuide: Choose firm produce that feels heavy for its size, with no soft, wet or mouldy patches. Choose heavy nuts with intact shells and no rattling kernel.
152.storageGuide: Keep in a cool, dry place and use promptly; discard chestnuts with mould or holes.
152.funFact: The edible chestnut belongs to the genus *Castanea*, whereas the familiar horse chestnut belongs to *Aesculus* and has inedible seeds. In Corsica, northern Italy, and France, chestnuts were ground into flour for breads and cakes.

default-152.name: Roasted Sweet Chestnuts
default-152.instructions: Score the shells, roast until the shells peel back, then peel while still warm. Fresh sweet chestnuts should be cooked or roasted before eating; do not confuse them with toxic horse chestnuts.

153.name: Daikon Radish
153.selectionGuide: Choose firm produce that feels heavy for its size, with no soft, wet or mouldy patches. Choose firm, smooth roots without soft spots or shrivelling.
153.storageGuide: Remove daikon greens if attached; refrigerate the unwashed root in a bag and wash before use.
153.funFact: Daikon is a key vegetable in Japanese, Korean, and Chinese cuisines. Grated raw daikon, called *daikon oroshi*, is served with dishes such as tempura and grilled fish because its fresh pungency balances rich foods.

default-153.name: Daikon Sesame Salad
default-153.instructions: Grate daikon and toss with rice vinegar, sesame oil and a little soy sauce.
default-153.raw: Peel if the skin is tough, then grate or slice thinly; both root and young leaves are edible.

154.name: Romanesco Cauliflower
154.selectionGuide: Choose crisp, fresh leaves with no slime, yellowing or extensive bruising. Choose a compact head with evenly coloured, tightly packed spirals.
154.storageGuide: Refrigerate unwashed Romanesco in a loose bag with the stem side down; use while the florets are firm.
154.funFact: Romanesco forms spiral cones arranged in a self-similar, fractal-like pattern. Its regular geometry comes from the development of the plant's meristem, whose successive growth stages repeat a similar arrangement.

default-154.name: Romanesco with Lemon and Hazelnuts
default-154.instructions: Steam the florets until just tender and finish with lemon, olive oil and toasted hazelnuts.
default-154.raw: Small, clean florets can be eaten raw after washing, although cooking is more common.

155.name: Black Radish
155.selectionGuide: Choose firm produce that feels heavy for its size, with no soft, wet or mouldy patches. Choose a firm root with intact dark skin and no soft spots.
155.storageGuide: Remove the tops from black radishes and refrigerate the unwashed roots in a perforated bag.
155.funFact: Black radish was traditionally grown in Europe as a winter vegetable because it stores well. Its pungency comes from glucosinolates, which break down after the root is cut to form mustard-like aromatic compounds.

default-155.name: Black Radish and Apple Slaw
default-155.instructions: Peel if the skin is tough, grate the root and mix with apple, lemon and yogurt for a sharp slaw.
default-155.raw: Peel if needed and grate or slice thinly; its flavour is stronger than that of pink radishes.

156.name: Scorzonera (Black Salsify)
156.selectionGuide: Choose firm produce that feels heavy for its size, with no soft, wet or mouldy patches. Choose firm roots without soft areas; latex may appear when cut.
156.storageGuide: Refrigerate unwashed scorzonera roots in a perforated bag to prevent drying; wash and peel before cooking.
156.funFact: Salsify is known as the 'black root'; its Polish name *wężymord* reflects an old belief that it could counter viper bites. Belgian and French cuisines prized it as a delicate vegetable with a flavor reminiscent of asparagus.

default-156.name: Lemon-Braised Scorzonera
default-156.instructions: Scrub and peel the roots, then simmer in lightly acidulated water until tender; serve with parsley and butter.
default-156.raw: It can be eaten raw when very young and tender, but it is usually peeled and cooked. Work with gloves if the milky sap is bothersome.

157.name: Sugar Snap Peas
157.selectionGuide: Choose firm produce that feels heavy for its size, with no soft, wet or mouldy patches. Pods should be bright green, crisp and full, with no yellowing.
157.storageGuide: Refrigerate unwashed sugar snap peas in a perforated bag; keep the pods dry and use soon.
157.funFact: Sugar snap peas combine traits of shelling peas and snow peas: they have sweet seeds and a fleshy edible pod. The English name *snap pea* refers to the crisp snap made by a fresh pod when broken.

default-157.name: Sugar Snap Peas with Garlic
default-157.instructions: Trim the stem ends and quickly sauté whole pods with garlic, lemon zest and sesame.
default-157.raw: The entire crisp pod is edible; remove any tough string and wash before eating.

158.name: Chanterelle Mushrooms
158.selectionGuide: Choose dry, firm chanterelles with intact edges and a mild earthy aroma; avoid slime or sour odors.
158.storageGuide: Refrigerate in a paper bag and brush clean just before cooking; avoid soaking wild mushrooms.
158.funFact: Chanterelles have blunt, forked ridges beneath the cap rather than the thin gills found on many mushrooms. Their yellow color and fruity aroma make them prized in northern European cuisines, especially in Scandinavia.

default-158.name: Butter-Sautéed Chanterelles
default-158.instructions: Brush off debris, tear large mushrooms and sauté slowly with butter, shallot and thyme until their liquid evaporates. Wild chanterelles should be cooked before eating; only eat mushrooms identified with certainty.

159.name: Porcini Mushrooms
159.selectionGuide: Choose porcini with firm stems and caps, no slime, sour odor, or extensive insect damage.
159.storageGuide: Refrigerate in a paper bag and use promptly; clean gently before cooking.
159.funFact: Porcini are bolete mushrooms: beneath the cap they have a layer of tiny tubes ending in pores, where spores form. Their characteristic umami flavor comes partly from free amino acids and nucleotides.

default-159.name: Porcini with Garlic and Parsley
default-159.instructions: Slice firm porcini and sauté with garlic and parsley; add a little pasta water for a glossy sauce. Cook porcini before eating and use only specimens identified with certainty.

160.name: Enoki Mushrooms
160.selectionGuide: Choose enoki with firm, pale stems in a compact cluster; avoid wet, slimy, or discolored mushrooms.
160.storageGuide: Keep refrigerated in the original pack, follow the use-by date and cook thoroughly.
160.funFact: Enoki is the cultivated form of the winter mushroom, which grows wild on dead wood and has a darker, shorter shape. The long white stems familiar in Asian cuisine are produced by growing it in low light and elevated carbon dioxide.

default-160.name: Thoroughly Cooked Enoki Soup
default-160.instructions: Trim the clustered base, separate the stems and add to soup or stir-fry near the end of cooking. Do not eat raw. Cook thoroughly and keep refrigerated; raw enoki has been associated with foodborne outbreaks.

161.name: Garden Cress
161.selectionGuide: Choose vivid, aromatic leaves with crisp stems and no dark or slimy patches. Choose fresh, green shoots without yellowing or excess moisture.
161.storageGuide: Keep cut garden cress cool in its growing tray or a covered container; avoid soaking it.
161.funFact: Garden cress belongs to the cabbage family, and its peppery flavor comes from products formed when glucosinolates break down. In Poland it is traditionally sown in spring, especially before Easter, on damp cotton wool or cellulose.

default-161.name: Garden Cress Sandwiches
default-161.instructions: Snip the fresh shoots over egg sandwiches, cottage cheese or a potato salad just before serving.
default-161.raw: Eat the washed shoots raw; grow or buy them for food rather than collecting unknown plants.

162.name: Aronia (Chokeberry)
162.selectionGuide: Choose plump berries with no leaking juice, mould or crushed fruit at the bottom of the pack. Choose fully dark berries with no mould or fermented smell.
162.storageGuide: Refrigerate briefly or freeze; the berries are usually cooked or juiced soon after picking.
162.funFact: Aronia is native to North America but has also become an important fruit crop in Poland. Its dark color comes from abundant anthocyanins, which give juices and preserves an intense ruby hue.

default-162.name: Aronia and Apple Compote
default-162.instructions: Simmer the washed berries with apple and a little water, then pass through a sieve for a tart sauce.
default-162.raw: ripe berries are edible raw, but they are very astringent; they are more often cooked, juiced or frozen.

163.name: Rosemary
163.selectionGuide: Choose fragrant rosemary sprigs with flexible stems and intact green-gray needles; avoid brittle, dry sprigs.
163.storageGuide: Wrap fresh rosemary loosely in a barely damp towel and refrigerate in a bag; keep it from becoming wet.
163.funFact: Rosemary belongs to the mint family, alongside mint, basil, and thyme. Its Latin name *Rosmarinus* is often interpreted as 'dew of the sea', a reference to the shrub's Mediterranean habitats.

default-163.name: Rosemary-Roasted Vegetables
default-163.instructions: Strip the leaves from woody stems, chop finely and add to roasted potatoes, beans or focaccia.
default-163.raw: but the leaves are tough and strongly flavoured; use them finely chopped in small amounts.

164.name: Thyme
164.selectionGuide: Choose thyme sprigs with a fresh aroma and green leaves; avoid yellowing or damp, blackened patches.
164.storageGuide: Refrigerate fresh thyme loosely wrapped in a dry paper towel inside a bag or container.
164.funFact: Thyme was used in ancient Greece and Rome both as a seasoning and in ritual practices. Its intense aroma comes partly from thymol, an essential-oil component with a distinctive herbal, spicy scent.

default-164.name: Thyme-Roasted Root Vegetables
default-164.instructions: Strip the small leaves from the stems and add to roasted roots, mushrooms or a lemon dressing.
default-164.raw: The tender leaves can be eaten raw in small amounts after washing; woody stems are usually discarded.

165.name: Oregano (Fresh)
165.selectionGuide: Choose fresh oregano with aromatic green leaves and firm stems; avoid wilted or blackened leaves.
165.storageGuide: Refrigerate fresh oregano loosely wrapped in a barely damp paper towel; keep leaves dry.
165.funFact: Oregano and marjoram belong to the genus *Origanum*, but differ in aroma and culinary use. Oregano is a foundation of Greek and southern Italian cooking, especially in dishes with tomatoes, olive oil, and grilled vegetables.

default-165.name: Tomato Salad with Fresh Oregano
default-165.instructions: Chop the fresh leaves into tomato salad or add them to olive oil with lemon and garlic.
default-165.raw: Wash and use the leaves raw or add them near the end of cooking.

166.name: Sage (Fresh)
166.selectionGuide: Choose sage with firm, aromatic gray-green leaves and no brown or slimy patches.
166.storageGuide: Wrap fresh sage loosely in a dry paper towel and refrigerate in a container; avoid excess moisture.
166.funFact: Sage was valued in antiquity; its Latin name *Salvia* comes from *salvare*, meaning 'to save' or 'to heal'. In Italian cooking, sage browned in butter makes an aromatic sauce for ravioli and gnocchi.

default-166.name: Crispy Sage Leaves
default-166.instructions: Fry whole leaves briefly in butter until crisp and serve over pumpkin or gnocchi.
default-166.raw: small amounts of washed fresh leaves can be eaten raw, but the strong flavour is usually better after cooking.

167.name: Lemongrass
167.selectionGuide: Choose firm, fragrant lemongrass stalks with pale bases; avoid dry, split, or mushy ends.
167.storageGuide: Wrap lemongrass stalks and refrigerate in a bag; freeze extra stalks for longer storage.
167.funFact: Lemongrass is a staple of Thai, Vietnamese, and Indonesian cuisines. Its citrus aroma comes mainly from citral, a mixture of fragrant compounds also found in lemon peel.

default-167.name: Lemongrass Soup
default-167.instructions: Bruise the lower stalks and simmer in a soup or tea; remove the fibrous stalks before serving.
default-167.raw: The tender inner core can be finely sliced, but the fibrous outer stalk is usually infused and removed rather than eaten raw.

168.name: Fresh Dates
168.selectionGuide: Choose plump, glossy dates with no fermentation smell or leaking.
168.storageGuide: Refrigerate ripe fresh dates in a covered container and use promptly.
168.funFact: Dates are the fruit of the date palm, one of the oldest cultivated plants of the Middle East. In many countries in the region they are served with coffee as a sign of hospitality; their natural sugars also make a sweet paste without added sugar.

default-168.name: Fresh Dates with Yogurt
default-168.instructions: Halve ripe dates, remove the stone and serve with plain yogurt, walnuts and a pinch of cinnamon.
default-168.raw: Eat the soft flesh raw and discard the hard stone; fresh dates are different from dried dates.

169.name: Lingonberries
169.selectionGuide: Choose plump berries with no leaking juice, mould or crushed fruit at the bottom of the pack. Choose firm red berries with no mould or crushed patches.
169.storageGuide: Refrigerate in a shallow ventilated container or freeze for longer storage.
169.funFact: Lingonberries are characteristic of the cool forests of northern Europe and Scandinavia. They contain natural benzoic acid, which inhibits some microorganisms and helps explain why the berries and their preserves keep well.

default-169.name: Lingonberry Preserve
default-169.instructions: Simmer the berries with a little sugar and water to make a tart preserve for roasted vegetables.
default-169.raw: ripe berries are edible raw but tart; they are often cooked into sauces or preserves.

170.name: Beet greens (young beet leaves)
170.selectionGuide: Choose bunches with firm, vivid-green leaves and no yellowing, slimy patches or mould. Any attached young beetroots should be firm and free of cracks.
170.storageGuide: Beet greens wilt quickly. Refrigerate them as soon as possible; leaves and small roots may be stored separately in a container or loose bag. Do not wash before storage and use promptly.

default-170.name: Classic beet greens soup
default-170.instructions: Wash the young beetroots, stems and leaves thoroughly. Dice and simmer the small roots in stock until tender; add the stems later and the leaves near the end, just until wilted. Season with dill, lemon juice and black pepper.
default-170.raw: Young, thoroughly washed leaves can be finely chopped into a salad; thicker stems and leaves are usually better briefly cooked.

170.funFact: Young beet greens, known in Polish as *botwina*, are the leaves and stalks harvested before the beet develops a large storage root. In Polish cuisine they are used in chilled soup and *botwinka*; their red pigments are betalains.

171.name: Sorrel
171.selectionGuide: Choose young, crisp green leaves without yellow patches, slime or signs of wilting. Smaller, tender leaves are usually less fibrous.
171.storageGuide: Refrigerate unwashed leaves, loosely wrapped in a slightly damp paper towel and placed in a container or bag. Wash just before use and use promptly.

default-171.name: Sorrel soup
default-171.instructions: Simmer potatoes and vegetables in stock. Finely chop the washed sorrel, add it near the end and cook briefly until the leaves soften. Season with black pepper and serve with a hard-boiled egg. Sorrel contains oxalic acid, which gives it its characteristic tart taste.
default-171.raw: young leaves can be added to a salad after thorough washing.

171.funFact: Sorrel gets its tart taste from organic acids, especially oxalic acid. It is a traditional ingredient in Central and Eastern European soups; dairy such as cream or eggs softens its pronounced acidity.

172.name: White currants
172.selectionGuide: Choose firm, plump, pale cream or slightly yellowish berries on fresh-looking trusses. Avoid mould, leaking juice and many crushed berries.
172.storageGuide: Keep unwashed, preferably on the trusses, in a shallow container in the refrigerator. Rinse and dry just before eating; surplus berries can be frozen after damaged fruit is removed.

default-172.name: White currant fruit salad
default-172.instructions: Rinse the trusses and pat them dry. Keep the berries on the stems for garnish or remove them gently with a fork; add to yogurt, porridge or a fruit salad.
default-172.raw: after washing; do not eat the tough stems.

172.funFact: White currant is a pale variety of the red currant, not a separate species. It usually has a milder flavor and lighter color because it contains far fewer red anthocyanin pigments.

173.name: Mirabelle plum
173.selectionGuide: Choose golden-yellow, ripe but firm fruit without splits, mould or extensive bruising. A natural bloom on the skin does not necessarily mean the fruit is spoiled.
173.storageGuide: Allow underripe fruit to ripen briefly at room temperature. Refrigerate ripe mirabelles and wash just before use; they are delicate and should be handled gently.

default-173.name: Roasted mirabelle plums
default-173.instructions: Wash the fruit, halve it and remove the stones. Place in a baking dish with a little water and cinnamon, then roast until tender. Serve with porridge, yogurt or dessert.
default-173.raw: after washing and removing the stone.

173.funFact: The mirabelle is a small-fruited variety of European plum, especially associated with Lorraine in France. The region uses it in tarts, preserves, and spirits, and its short season is an important part of local food tradition.

174.name: Rose hips
174.selectionGuide: Choose ripe, deep-red or orange-red hips that are firm and undamaged. Avoid mouldy or rotting fruit and fruit from polluted areas; when foraging, make sure the species is correctly identified.
174.storageGuide: Process fresh hips promptly or keep them briefly in a ventilated container in the refrigerator. Before drying or freezing, remove the stalks and remaining flower parts; when preparing the pulp, remove the seeds and irritating hairs.

default-174.name: Rose hip purée
default-174.instructions: Wash the hips and remove the stalks and remaining flower parts. Simmer in a little water until soft, then pass through a very fine sieve to separate the seeds and irritating hairs. Use the pulp for purée, syrup or jam.
default-174.raw: Do not eat the uncleaned inside of the fruit; the seeds and hairs must be thoroughly separated from the pulp.

174.funFact: Rose hips are among the richest natural sources of vitamin C, although levels vary by species and processing method. In Europe they have long been made into preserves, syrups, and infusions, especially for autumn and winter.

20b.name: Garlic
20b.selectionGuide: Firm, tight skin, heavy for size. Avoid if cloves feel hollow or soft.
20b.storageGuide: Keep in a dry, dark, well-ventilated space at room temperature. A mesh bag or open basket is ideal.
20b.funFact: When garlic is crushed, the enzyme alliinase converts alliin into allicin, the compound responsible for its pungent aroma. As with onions and horseradish, the strong smell appears only after the plant's cells are damaged.

default-20b.name: Classic Garlic recipe
default-20b.instructions: Roast a whole garlic bulb until soft; squeeze the cloves into mashed potatoes.
default-20b.raw: use small amounts if its sharp flavor is too strong.
